full_judgment:
"Whether in the facts and circumstances of the case, the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified in upholding the DCT's assessment of capital gains on the applicant on his transfer of property to H & Z Complex Ltd. and whether the applicant made any profits/gains arising from such transfer, within the meaning of section 31 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984?" 

 6. Mr. Fida M. Kamal, the learned Counsel representing the applicant, has contended that the assessee applicant has not made any gain or profit out of the transfer made by the assessee and his wife in respect of their jointly owned land and building to the company which was constituted for the purpose of carrying on business of real properties and particularly for the purpose of earning profit by letting out the flats of the building standing on the land. He has further argued that in commercial and economic sense the transfer does not constitute any business transaction and by that transaction the assessee neither earned any profit nor gained anything in terms of money and the transfer made by the applicant being an investment to the company in terms of having purchased some shares of the company of which the applicant is a shareholder director. It is contended that the Taxes Appellate Tribunal failed to appreciate that the assessee did not make any profit or gain out of the transaction i.e. sale of land and building by registered instrument dated 28.8.91 and consequently the Tribunal was not justified in upholding the assessment order as regards capital gain. He has made reliance in the case of Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Public Industries reported in 1969 P.T.D. page 622 where a Division Bench of the Karachi High Court in the context of section 10(2)(vii) of the Income Tax Act 1922 and considering various decision on the question raised as to whether a partnership firm converting itself into a private limited company and transferring its assets to whether a partnership firm converting itself into a private limited company and transferring its assets to such company at cost price can be held to be not a sale as to attract provision of 2nd proviso to section 10(2)(vii) of the Act. It has been stated in paragraph 14 in the following terms: 

 "The majority view is that if the partners of a firm decide to float a company transferring their assets in the firm to the new company such a transfer is not a sale. The contrary view would be a clog in changing the business of firms to corporate bodies, and they would be hampered from converting themselves into limited companies and perhaps this may lead to some undesirable devices which the promoters of the new company may have to adopt for that purpose. We need not repeat the well known principle followed by the majority Courts that no person can himself be a buyer and seller and commercially, it is not possible that such a sale, if at all, by any stretch of imagination, could be considered as one would result into any profit, and unless profit is made, such a transferor would not come within the mischief of section 10(2)(vii) of the Income Tax Act. Legally no doubt, it is true that a uompany is a separate entity from the subscribers of the company but logically and commercially it makes no sense at all that when partners in a firm decide to float a new company with almost the same shares in the new company to the extent of their shares in the firm they would be buyers and sellers of their own interest. The assets and liabilities of the firm are transferred to the company, but as shareholders of the company their liabilities though limited but it is limited to the extent of their shares in the old firm. In view of the matter, we fail to understand how this act of persons who being transferors of their shares in a firm to the new company which allots them shares to the extent of their interest in the firm can be termed as a "sale", which can result in any profit." 

 7. Reliance has also been placed in the case of M/s A.K. Khan Plywood Co. Chittagong vs. The Commissioner of Income Tax, East Pakistan reported in 25 DLR(SC) 65, where the simple fact was that the partnership firm M/s. A.K. Khan Plywood Co. sold its running business together with assets and liabilities to the private limited company as M/s. A.K. Khan Plywood Co. Ltd. The question arose whether any profit resulted from the transfer so made. It was held as under:- 

 "The transaction between the partnership firm and the private limited company was not a business transaction entered into with the object of earning a profit. The profit said to have resulted from the transaction was only a book entry and not a profit from the commercial point of view. It was not, therefore, a sale in the real sense of the term. The procedure followed was only for the purpose of re-adjustment of the position of the partners as holders of the shares of the private limited company. By forming a private limited company, the partners only adopted a different method of carrying on the same business. The assessee firm, therefore, did not make any profit or gain so as to bring the case within the mischief of the second proviso to section 10(2)(vii) of the Act." 

 In that case the principle laid down in william Richard Doughty vs. Commissioner of Taxes, reported in A.I.R 1927 (P.C) 76 was referred to which is in the following terms:- 

 8. Mr. Sarder Jinnat Ali, the learned assistant Attorney General, has appeared on behalf of the revenue and he has contended that the transfer of land and building was made by the assessee and his wife by undervaluing the deed and that was detected by the assessing officer the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes on investigation and verification of the actual price of the land. The learned Assistant Attorney General has pointed out that according to the valuation as shown in the statement of assets and liabilities the construction costs of the building is Tk. 1,69,94,110/- and that was taken to be the price of the building; Tk. 31,26,924/- as disclosed in the return was taken to be the value of the land and the assessee and his wife transferred the property worth of over Tk. two crores at a nominal price of Tk. 14,00,000 showing purchase of 14000 shares valued at Tk. 14,00,000/- and he submitted that the asessee has made gain out of the transaction which is liable to be taxed under the provision of section 32 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. It is contended that if the fair market value of the land is determined even at the admitted price as disclosed in the statement the assessee has definitely made gain out of the transaction. He has further argued that the transfer that was made by the assessee to a company which is a juristic person and as such the cited cases are not attracted as in the those cases the partners of partnership firm transferred the assets and liabilities of the firm to the company formed by the partners. The principle laid down in those cases are not at all applicable in view of the facts of the present case. 

 9. We have given our anxious consideration to the submission made by the learned Counsel representing the applicant as well as the learned Assistant Attorney General. In this particular case the question which requires our utmost consideration is whether the assessee applicant has gained anything out of the transaction by which their jointly owned land and building was transferred to the company, namely, H & Z Complex Ltd. of which the assessee and his wife are the shareholders directors. The company was constituted by the husband and wife, which can be said to be a family company. The property belonged to the husband and wife and they have invested the said property in their business by way of transfer in terms of shares of the said company. Admittedly the assessee applicant obtained 7000 shares valued at Tk. 7,00,000/-and the wife who is also the director share-holder obtained 7000 shares of the same value for her portion of the property transferred to the company. The deed in respect of the transfer was registered in accordance with the provision of law on payment of proper stamp duty and income tax. No tangible evidence is there to show that the assessee by the said transfer except acquisition of certain shares of the company has gained the amount as shown in the assessment order. Virtually, the transfer made by the assessee and his wife to the company is a kind of investment in their business in terms of having some shares in the company and the assessee cannot be said to have gained anything out of the transaction. The principle expounded in the aforesaid cited cases can be analogically deduced add can apply in the instant case for inasmuch as the assessee applicant has not gained out of the transaction. By that transfer even if the value of the property is found to be much more than what has been shown in the deed of transfer. the assets of the company may have been increased but the assessee has not gained anything as the transfer did not give rise to any profit or gain and since the assessee has not earned any profit gain the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was not justified in upholding the order of assessment.
